title: Sensitivity bars (tornado) and Sobol indices: which inputs drive the output?
summary: Which inputs drive the output? A tornado chart shows the swing of the output when each input is moved alone between low and high values; Sobol indices show the share of the output variance that each input explains, with confidence intervals.

media.alt: Two panels sharing input names k1 to k7 sorted from largest at the top: left, a tornado chart of horizontal bars around a baseline output of 10 with rose for low inputs and teal for high; right, paired horizontal bars of first-order index S1 (teal) and total index ST (blue, hatched) with 95 percent error bars, from 0.38 and 0.45 for k1 down to 0.01 and 0.02 for k7.
media.caption: Reference render of class F8.5 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Which inputs drive the output?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: output (unit) from about 9.3 to 10.7 on x, with a vertical line at the base value 10; one row per input. Right: Sobol index from 0 to 0.5 on x for the same rows; error bars are 95 percent confidence intervals.
look_at: Are the rows sorted by importance, with the largest swing on top?
Do the tornado and the Sobol ranking agree?
How much larger is the total index than the first-order index for each input (interactions)?
Do the confidence intervals of neighbouring inputs overlap, so their order is uncertain?
as_drawn: Tornado: the output at the base point is 10; swings (high minus low) are k1 1.17, k2 0.87, k3 0.56, k4 0.52, k5 0.30, k6 0.14, k7 0.08; the bars are asymmetric (for k3 -0.18 below and +0.38 above).
Sobol indices S1 = 0.38, 0.27, 0.14, 0.08, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01 sum to 0.95; total indices ST = 0.45, 0.36, 0.19, 0.11, 0.07, 0.03, 0.02 are larger for every input.
Confidence half-widths are about 0.04 for k1 down to 0.01 for k7; k4 and k5 (0.08 and 0.05) have overlapping intervals, as do k6 and k7.
The tornado does not say what low and high mean (the input ranges), and the rows are sorted by swing in both panels.
read_the_figure.proves: The ranking says which inputs matter most over the ranges used. The Sobol indices additionally say what share of the output variance each input accounts for, alone and with interactions. Neither says anything about inputs outside the ranges.
if_wrong: Unsorted bars: the reader must hunt for the largest; always sort.
Indices without intervals: the ranking of close values is not reliable.
A tornado of a model with strong interactions: the one-at-a-time swings are misleading; look at ST - S1.
must_check: sorted: the purpose is to find what matters most, so the largest must be first.
confidence intervals: Sobol indices are estimated from samples and have noise; without intervals the ranks of near neighbours cannot be trusted.

terms.meaning: Bars showing the change in the output when each input is moved alone from its low to its high value, sorted by size.
Varying one input with the others fixed at their base values; a local picture around the base point.
The share of the output variance explained by one input alone.
The share of the variance in which the input takes part, alone or in interaction.
A joint effect of inputs that is not the sum of their separate effects; the gap between ST and S1 reveals it.
The range within which the true index lies with 95 percent confidence, given the sampling noise.

remember: S_i is at most S_Ti; the gap is the interaction involvement of input i.
The sum of S_i is at most 1; 1 minus the sum is the interaction share.
The sum of S_Ti is at least 1 (interactions are counted for each participant).
A tornado is local and misses interactions; Sobol indices are global.
Always sort and always give intervals.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Left: each row is an input; the bar to the left (rose) shows the output when that input is low and the bar to the right (teal) when it is high, both measured from the base value at the vertical line. Right: for each input two bars, solid teal for the first-order index and hatched blue for the total index, with thin error bars; rows are in the same order in both panels. Hatching separates the two indices beyond colour.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: when a result depends on many inputs, you want to know which to measure carefully and which to ignore. Moving each input alone and recording the effect gives a quick ranking and the tornado shape is that ranking at a glance. Variance-based indices go further by saying what share of the output's uncertainty comes from each input, including their combined effects, which tells you where reducing uncertainty will pay off.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: The tornado depends on the low and high values chosen, which are not shown, and on the base point: at another base point the order may change. It cannot see interactions. Sobol indices assume independent inputs, are estimated with noise (the intervals), and tell nothing about non-influential inputs beyond the ranges tested. Close neighbours (k4 and k5, k6 and k7) cannot be ranked from these intervals.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A scatter plot of the output against each input with a smooth trend shows non-linear shapes that an index hides. Morris screening ranks inputs cheaply before a full Sobol analysis. A table of S1, ST and their intervals is the exact version of the right panel.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Print the low and high input values beside each tornado bar, shade the interaction share (ST - S1) as a third segment, and add an extra marker row for the sum of indices so the reader can check the budget.

worked.title: Reading the sensitivity analysis of the reference render
worked.problem: (1) Which input has the largest swing and what is it? (2) What share of the variance do the first two inputs explain alone and in total? (3) How much variance is due to interactions?

solution.text: (1) k1: the bar runs from 9.38 to 10.55 around the base of 10.
(2) First-order indices 0.38 and 0.27 give 65 percent alone. The total indices are 0.45 and 0.36.
(3) The unexplained share of the first-order indices is the interaction share.

worked.answer: k1 with a swing of 1.17; k1 and k2 explain 65 percent of the variance alone and are involved in 81 percent in total; interactions account for 5 percent of the variance.

analyze.q: ST is larger than S1 for every input. What does it tell you about the model?
The tornado bars for k3 are asymmetric. What does that suggest about the response to k3?
Which two inputs could you swap in the ranking without contradicting the intervals?

evaluate.q: You decide to ignore k6 and k7 because their indices are small. Is that safe?

create: Redraw the tornado with the input values printed beside each bar.
Add a third segment to each Sobol bar for ST - S1 and a marker for the budget (the sum).

checks.q: What is the difference between S_i and S_Ti?
checks.answer: S_i is the variance share explained by input i alone; S_Ti includes all the effects in which i takes part, including interactions, so S_Ti is at least S_i.

checks.q: First-order indices 0.5, 0.3, 0.1. What is the interaction share at most?
checks.answer: 1 - 0.9 = 0.1, so at most 10 percent of the variance comes from interactions.

checks.q: A tornado ranks A above B, but the Sobol indices rank B above A. Give a possible reason.
checks.answer: The tornado is local at the base point with chosen ranges, while the Sobol analysis averages over the whole input distribution including interactions; B may matter more away from the base point or through interactions with other inputs.
